771.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
771.explanation: King Nami answers Indra's call to subdue rival princes by ranking conquest of the self above any number of battlefield victories.
771.tie_back: The Kural's warrior boasts of the many foes his lord has turned into memorial stones, and Jainism answers that boast with a greater victory, one won over oneself.
771.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
771._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It addresses the same theme of conquest but deliberately reverses the Kural's martial pride, so it is a contrast rather than a parallel.

772.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness.” … “difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
772.explanation: Nami names the self, with the senses, anger, pride, delusion and greed, as the hardest enemy of all and the only one worth fighting.
772.tie_back: The Kural honours the warrior who aims at the mighty elephant rather than the easy hare, and Jainism likewise chooses the hardest adversary, the self, over lesser foes.
772.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.35–36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
772._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (two excerpts joined with an ellipsis). The shared idea is choosing the worthiest opponent; in the Jain text that opponent is internal and no outward battle is approved.

773.quote_or_event: In Hemacandra's account of the duel between the brothers Bharata and Bahubali, Bahubali raises his fist for a blow that would have crushed Bharata. He then stops himself, turns the same hand to pluck out his own hair in the ascetic's renunciation, and gives up the kingdom instead of striking his defeated brother.
773.explanation: Jain tradition makes this moment of restraint toward a beaten rival, not the victory, the climax of Bahubali's heroism; he goes on to become a revered kevalin.
773.tie_back: The Kural calls kindness to an enemy in misfortune the 'sharp edge' of valour, and Bahubali's mercy to the brother at his feet is the best-known Jain example of exactly that.
773.source: Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.5 (Ādīśvaracaritra, 'The fight between Bharata and Bāhubali'), tr. Helen M. Johnson; wisdomlib.org
773._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the episode was confirmed through wisdomlib's Johnson translation listing and other summaries, but no wording is quoted. A strong thematic fit, though in Jainism the mercy ends in renunciation rather than generosity on the battlefield.

774.quote_or_event: “If any misfortune happens and he suffers pain, he should cheerfully steady his mind, and bear the ills that attack him.”
774.explanation: Among the hardships a monk must bear is bodily suffering, which he is to meet calmly and with good cheer instead of complaint.
774.tie_back: The Kural's hero pulls an enemy spear from his own body and smiles, and the Jain monk is likewise told to meet pain in his body with a cheerful, steady mind.
774.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
774._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It matches cheerful endurance of pain, but there is no weapon or battle, and the Jain point is passionless forbearance, not fighting spirit.

775.quote_or_event: “In a burial-place, or a deserted house, or below a tree he should sit down, alone, without moving, and he should not drive away any one. Sitting there he should brave all dangers; when seized with fear, he should not rise and go to some other place.”
775.explanation: A monk meditating alone must not move from his seat even when danger and fear come; leaving it would be a retreat.
775.tie_back: The Kural says that for the truly brave even a blink before a flying spear counts as flight, and the Jain rule likewise treats the smallest yielding to fear as a failure of nerve.
775.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 2.20–21 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
775._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. A strong fit on not flinching from danger in the slightest; the context is meditation, not combat.

776.quote_or_event: “Acquire perfect knowledge of the Law! why do you not study it? It is difficult to obtain instruction in it after this life. The days (that are gone by) will never return, nor is it easy a second time to obtain human birth.”
776.explanation: Rishabha warns his sons that each day not used for the Law is lost for good, because human birth is rare.
776.tie_back: The Kural's hero counts every day without an honourable wound as wasted, and the Jain teaching likewise reckons each day by whether it was spent in hard spiritual effort.
776._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It shares the idea of reckoning days and counting idle ones as lost, but the measure is study of the Law, not wounds taken in battle.

777.quote_or_event: “But famous warriors, leaders of heroes at the time of the battle, do not look behind them; (they think) what if all end with death?”
777.explanation: Unlike the coward who looks for a hiding-place, the true warrior fights without caring for his life, and the monk is told to 'exert himself in a similar way' (1.3.3.7).
777.tie_back: The Kural says the hero's anklet belongs only to those who do not cling to life, and the Sutrakritanga uses the same warrior's indifference to death as its model of resolve.
777._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. A close fit on heroes who do not cling to life, though the text uses the warrior only as a simile for the monk and says nothing of fame or the anklet.

778.quote_or_event: “He who always acknowledges his allegiance to his teacher, who has religious zeal and ardour for study, who is kind in words and actions, deserves to be instructed.”
778.explanation: The ideal disciple combines steady loyalty to his teacher with zeal of his own that does not fade.
778.tie_back: The Kural's warriors keep their ardour even when the king angrily holds them back, and the Jain disciple likewise joins obedience to his superior with undimmed zeal.
778.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 11.14 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
778._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. This is a next-best match: obedience together with zeal is shared, but there is no rebuke or restraint by the superior, and no war.

779.quote_or_event: “These two ways of life ending with death have been declared: death with one's will, and death against one's will. Death against one's will is that of ignorant men, and it happens (to the same individual) many times. Death with one's will is that of wise men, and at best it happens but once.”
779.explanation: Mahavira praises the wise man's 'death with one's will', which in Jain practice is the vow of sallekhana kept to the end (5.31–32), and sets it against the fool's frightened death.
779.tie_back: The Kural says no one can blame those who die keeping the vow they made, and Jainism likewise honours the one who keeps his vow until death as having died the best death.
779.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.2–3 (cf. 5.31–32) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
779._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Death in fidelity to a vow is a real parallel, but the Jain vow is non-violent renunciation, never a battle-oath, and the two must not be equated.

780.quote_or_event: “A wise man having weighed (both kinds of death) and chosen the better one (taught in) the Law of Compassion, will become calm through patience, with an undisturbed mind (at the time of death).”
780.explanation: The wise man deliberately chooses the right kind of death and meets it calmly.
780.tie_back: The Kural calls a hero's death that brings tears to his king's eyes worth begging for, and the Jain text also treats a good death as something to be sought and chosen, though it measures that death by inner calm and compassion rather than by a patron's grief.
780.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 5.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
780._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. This is a next-best match: both treat a worthy death as something to seek, but Jainism does not glorify death in war or measure it by a king's grief.
